title: Lotus Sutra 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer introduces the Lotus Sutra by tracing its rise within Mahayana Buddhism, then reads chapter 1 and the start of chapter 2 ("Expedient Means"). Norman describes Kumarajiva's 406 translation and the Tiantai school's ordering of the teachings. In chapter 1, a beam of light from the Buddha's forehead prompts Maitreya's question, and Manjushri answers with the story of the Buddha Sun Moon Bright, in which Maitreya was once the slacker Seeker of Fame. In chapter 2, five thousand listeners walk out as the Buddha says only a Buddha and a Buddha can understand the one great causal condition. Norman ends on the little boys piling sand into Buddha towers.

sentences.text: A few months ago, we were studying sutras from the Pali Canon, which were probably the earliest sayings of the Buddha in the ancient style.

Then, probably around the first century, or around maybe earlier than that, there was some sort of spurt of tremendous enthusiasm that arose right in the middle of Buddhism.

That was very much about compassion and love for the Buddha and devotion to the Buddha as a person, and tremendous creativity and imagination—characteristics that were not exactly emphasized in the earlier original teachings of the Buddha, but were not absent either.
They were there, but not emphasized.
These tendencies came out really strongly and powerfully, and that's the movement that came to be called Mahayana Buddhism, the great vehicle.
The Lotus Sutra is one of the most important sutras of the Mahayana tendency, the Mahayana literature.
It's by far the most important single Buddhist sutra in the Far East, that means in China, in Japan, Korea.
The Lotus Sutra sort of has a unique position in all those cultures for some reason, not so much in India and in Sanskrit.
It seems like the Lotus Sutra is a Sanskrit text.
Remember when we talked about the Surya and Gama Sutra, we were doubting, at least I was doubting, whether it really ever existed in Sanskrit.
Maybe it was written in Chinese.
The Lotus Sutra probably was, the scholars think, written originally in Sanskrit.
But most of the Sanskrit texts, I think, original texts are lost, and I believe that the Sanskrit texts that are existing now are not as old as the earliest Chinese texts.
That doesn't mean it didn't exist in earlier versions of Sanskrit.
But the famous translator, Kumarajiva, who I think I talked about when we talked about Surya and Gama Sutra, he was a very famous translator.
His translation bureau was kind of like to China, what the King James committee that wrote the King James Bible, translated the Bible into English, is to the Christian West.

Somehow he managed to get together the most elegant and powerful literary minds of China to render the Lotus Sutra into Chinese in a beautiful language that was very much characteristic of Chinese as a language and a culture.
So it was a great literary feat, the same way the King James Bible is a literary feat.
So it became, because of that, and because of what it teaches, it became really famous and really important throughout the Far East.
His translation was made in the year 406.
And the school of Buddhism called Tiantai, or Tendai in Japanese, which is a really powerful Buddhist school, focused itself on the Lotus Sutra as its primary text.

It recognized numerous texts and had numerous practices and rituals.
I mean, it was a really complicated and full school in China, and it was transmitted to Japan as Tendai.
